blocks.text: Move data across a boundary in a simple object shaped for that boundary, not in your domain object.

A **DTO** has fields and no behavior. It exists so that a remote call, a screen or a message gets exactly the data it needs in a stable shape. An **assembler** or mapper converts between DTOs and domain objects at the edge, keeping internals, secrets and lazy associations from leaking.

items: **Shape:** one DTO per use case or contract.
**Content:** primitives, strings, nested DTOs, no entities.
**Direction:** request DTOs in, response DTOs out.

blocks.text: A Java record is a natural DTO: immutable, equality by value, and a compact constructor for boundary validation.

Two records: an outbound summary with only what the client needs, and an inbound request that validates at construction.
The assembler is the only code that knows both shapes. It converts the entity to the summary and a request into a new entity.
The boundary code deals only in DTOs; the entity is created from the request and summarized for output.

blocks.text: A public REST API over a legacy orders schema.

The database has 40 columns per order, internal status codes and lazy-loaded relations. The public contract exposes `OrderResponse` with id, status text, line items and totals, versioned as `v1` and `v2`. A mapper isolates the legacy schema; renaming a column or adding an internal flag leaves `v1` clients untouched.

lists.title: Use when
items: You expose an API whose contract must outlive the domain model.
One call should return data from several aggregates in a single round trip.
Entities hold secrets, lazy associations or cycles.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Layers are in the same process and the entity is already the right shape.
A DTO would be a field-for-field copy of an entity with no boundary reason.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Behavior added to DTOs, which turns them into a second domain model.
Mapping code scattered across controllers instead of one assembler.
Reusing one DTO for requests and responses, coupling both directions.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Copies of the same fields at every layer: entity, model, dto, view, resource.
Mappers with `null` checks for every field because no one owns the contract.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records replace most hand-written DTO classes.
Sealed interfaces model a versioned payload that has several variants.

rows.difference: A data mapper moves data between entities and the database. A DTO assembler does the same between entities and the API. Different edges, same discipline.
A facade exposes a coarse-grained service API and typically returns DTOs so callers never see domain internals.
Both snapshot state in a plain object. A memento is opaque and exists to restore its originator; a DTO is readable and exists to inform another party.
DTOs are best immutable so they can be shared across threads and cached safely.
A repository returns domain aggregates to the domain. DTOs are produced after it, at the outer boundary, not by it.

exercises.prompt: Explain DTOs: what they carry, where they are created, and why not expose entities directly.

modelAnswer.text: A DTO is a plain, ideally immutable object that carries data across a boundary in a shape defined for that boundary. A mapper at the edge converts between DTOs and domain objects. Exposing entities leaks secrets, lazy proxies and internal structure, and couples the public contract to your model.

keyPoints: Plain data carrier with no behavior
Shaped for the boundary or use case
Entities leak secrets and lazy state
Records are the idiomatic Java form
